tenancy_law.rule: Rent increases must be reasonable and subject to mutual agreement. Unilateral increases without notice are generally unenforceable. Courts have held that increases beyond 10-15% per annum without justification are unconscionable.
tenancy_law.negotiation_tip: Negotiate a fixed rent review cap tied to Nigeria's CPI/inflation rate, not landlord discretion. A mutual 90-day notice period is standard.

tenancy_law.statute: Common Law & Lagos State Tenancy Law 2011
tenancy_law.rule: The Landlord is responsible for all external, structural, and major repairs. This includes the roof, load-bearing walls, foundation, and external plumbing. A clause shifting this burden to the tenant without compensatory rent reduction is void.
tenancy_law.negotiation_tip: Reject clauses that assign structural repairs to the Tenant. If accepted, negotiate a significant rent reduction or a one-time capital allowance.

tenancy_law.statute: Recovery of Premises Act Cap R4 LFN 2004 & Lagos State Tenancy Law 2011
tenancy_law.rule: A yearly tenant is entitled to 6 months' notice to quit. A half-yearly tenant gets 3 months, a quarterly tenant gets 1.5 months, and a monthly tenant gets 1 month. Any clause waiving this statutory right is void and unenforceable.
tenancy_law.negotiation_tip: Ensure the notice period in the contract aligns with the Recovery of Premises Act. Do not sign any clause that says the Landlord can require immediate vacation.

tenancy_law.statute: Recovery of Premises Act & Criminal Code Act
tenancy_law.rule: Self-help eviction (locking the tenant out, removing belongings) is illegal in Nigeria. The Landlord must obtain a court order. A clause purporting to authorize self-help eviction is void.
tenancy_law.negotiation_tip: Flag any clause that allows the Landlord to 're-enter' the premises without a court order. This is a criminal offense under Nigerian law.

tenancy_law.statute: Lagos State Tenancy Law 2011 & Common Law
tenancy_law.rule: A tenant's repair obligation at lease end is limited to 'fair wear and tear' unless they caused actual damage. Clauses requiring the tenant to return premises to 'original condition' or fund full refurbishment go beyond what Nigerian courts will enforce.
tenancy_law.negotiation_tip: Add 'fair wear and tear excepted' to every repair and reinstatement clause. Commission and attach a schedule of condition at signing.

tenancy_law.rule: A landlord may only retain the security deposit to the extent of actual, documented damage or unpaid rent. Blanket forfeiture clauses — where the deposit is automatically forfeited on any breach, however minor — are unfair under Nigerian law.
tenancy_law.negotiation_tip: Insist the deposit refund clause specifies an itemized deduction statement must be provided within 30 days of vacating, with any balance returned promptly. Undocumented forfeitures are challengeable.
red_flags: landlord may retain the entire deposit
deposit forfeited in event of breach

tenancy_law.rule: An absolute prohibition on subletting or assignment without landlord consent is common but should not entitle the landlord to withhold consent unreasonably. Consent should not be unreasonably delayed or conditioned on payment of a fee.
tenancy_law.negotiation_tip: Change 'shall not sublet' to 'shall not sublet without landlord's written consent, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld or delayed.' Remove any subletting premium fee clauses.

commercial_law.statute: Nigerian Contract Law (Common Law principles applied by Nigerian courts)
commercial_law.rule: A clause is a void penalty if it imposes a payment on breach disproportionate to the innocent party's loss. Only 'Liquidated Damages' — a genuine pre-estimate of loss — are enforceable. Nigerian courts consistently strike down punitive penalties.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Replace 'penalty' with 'Liquidated Damages' language. Both parties should agree on a reasonable daily rate tied to actual project costs, not a punitive multiplier.

commercial_law.statute: Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) 2020, Section 301
commercial_law.rule: Any provision exempting a company director from liability for negligence or breach of duty is void. A one-sided indemnity that only protects the stronger party exposes the weaker party to unlimited risk and is contrary to natural justice principles applied by Nigerian courts.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Demand mutual indemnity clauses. Any waiver of rights for 'supplier negligence' or 'landlord negligence' must be removed — this is a void provision under CAMA 2020 principles.
red_flags: waives all rights to claim damages

commercial_law.statute: Copyright Act 2022 (Nigeria)
commercial_law.rule: Copyright ownership initially vests in the author/creator. For commissioned works, an explicit written assignment is required to transfer full ownership. A vague 'work-for-hire' clause may not transfer copyright under the Nigerian Copyright Act 2022.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Ensure the IP clause explicitly states: (a) what IP is being assigned, (b) that it covers future works created during the contract, and (c) that you retain your pre-existing tools, frameworks, and background IP.

commercial_law.statute: Standard Nigerian Commercial Practice & Common Law
commercial_law.rule: Contracts should provide mutual termination rights. A clause allowing only the stronger party to terminate at will, while locking in the other party, creates an unconscionable imbalance that courts may refuse to enforce.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Insist on a mutual 30-day 'termination for convenience' clause. If the other party terminates early, you should be entitled to pro-rata payment for work done plus a break fee.

commercial_law.statute: Nigerian Arbitration and Conciliation Act 2023
commercial_law.rule: A clause specifying a foreign jurisdiction for dispute resolution for a contract fully performed in Nigeria is practically unenforceable and extremely costly to litigate. The new Nigerian Arbitration and Conciliation Act 2023 promotes local arbitration.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Ensure the governing law is 'Federal Republic of Nigeria' and dispute resolution specifies Lagos Multi-Door Courthouse (LMDC) or Lagos Court of Arbitration (LCA) for cost-effective resolution.
red_flags: governed by the laws of england

commercial_law.statute: Nigerian Contract Law & Restraint of Trade Doctrine
commercial_law.rule: An overly broad non-compete clause is unenforceable in Nigeria if it is unreasonable as to geographic scope, time duration, or the activity restricted. Nigerian courts will not enforce restraints that effectively prevent a person from earning a living.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Non-compete clauses should be limited to 6-12 months, within a defined geographic radius, and restricted to only directly competing businesses — not entire industries.
red_flags: shall not engage in any business

commercial_law.statute: Nigerian Commercial Practice & Common Law
commercial_law.rule: A clause imposing mandatory purchase minimums backed by automatic shortfall penalty fees or cascade termination is an illegal penalty clause under Nigerian law unless tied to genuine pre-estimated losses.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Cap shortfall fees to actual documented losses, insert a grace period, and permit shortfall carrying-forward to future quarters.
red_flags: penalty fee for failure to purchase

commercial_law.statute: Sale of Goods Law & CAMA 2020
commercial_law.rule: Romalpa-style clauses granting immediate forfeiture or repossession of delivered goods upon minor payment default create high risk for distributors and may violate Nigerian equity principles. Courts require a reasonable cure period before repossession rights activate.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Insist on written notice of default with a minimum 14-day cure period before repossession or title forfeiture rights trigger.
red_flags: goods remain the property of the supplier

commercial_law.statute: Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act (FCCPA) 2018
commercial_law.rule: Automatic renewal by silence or deemed acceptance of unilateral price changes without explicit affirmative written consent is unfair under Nigerian consumer and commercial protection standards.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Require written notice 30 days prior to any renewal or price adjustment, with explicit opt-out rights.
red_flags: unless written notice is given to the contrary

commercial_law.statute: Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act (FCCPA) 2018 & Nigerian Contract Law
commercial_law.rule: A clause permitting one party to vary the contract price at its sole discretion, with the other party's continued performance treated as acceptance, violates the basic contract principle that variation requires fresh consideration and mutual consent. Nigerian courts and the FCCPA treat such clauses as unfair terms.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Replace with a fixed pricing schedule for the contract term. If price reviews are needed, require mutual written agreement, minimum 60 days advance notice, and an explicit right to terminate without penalty if the new price is unacceptable.
red_flags: price may be adjusted at any time
continued purchase shall constitute acceptance of the new price
supplier reserves the right to amend prices
adjust its prices without prior consent

commercial_law.statute: Nigerian Contract Law & Restraint of Trade Doctrine
commercial_law.rule: A distribution agreement granting the supplier unlimited rights to appoint additional distributors in the same territory — without compensation, right of first refusal, or territorial protection — renders the distributorship commercially valueless and may be unconscionable where the distributor has invested significantly in market development.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Negotiate defined territorial exclusivity, or a right of first refusal before new distributors are appointed, plus compensation for lost market share if the territory is split. At minimum, cap the number of competing distributors the supplier can appoint in your territory.

commercial_law.statute: Sale of Goods Act (applicable in Nigeria) & Common Law
commercial_law.rule: A clause that exempts the supplier from all liability for late or failed delivery while simultaneously making the distributor's payment obligations 'of the essence' (i.e., time-critical) creates a fundamental and unenforceable imbalance. Both parties' core obligations should carry equivalent consequences for breach.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Insist on matching time-of-the-essence provisions: if payment timing is of the essence, delivery timing must be equally strict, with liquidated damages for late delivery equivalent to any late-payment interest rate charged to the distributor.
red_flags: supplier shall not be liable for delay
time shall be of the essence for payment
payment obligations are strictly of the essence
distributor shall not withhold payment due to delivery delay
failure to deliver shall not entitle
payment shall not be conditional on delivery

commercial_law.statute: Nigerian Contract Law & Equity
commercial_law.rule: A clause granting one party the unilateral right to set off any amount it claims is owed — against payments otherwise due to the other party, without notice, without agreement, and before the underlying claim is proved — is an unfair term. Nigerian courts require set-off rights to be mutual, disclosed, and limited to liquidated (ascertained) debts.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Remove unilateral set-off rights or replace with: 'Neither party may exercise set-off without 14 days prior written notice specifying the amounts and basis of the set-off, and only in respect of undisputed, liquidated debts.' Ensure set-off rights are mutual.
red_flags: deduct from amounts payable to the distributor

commercial_law.statute: CAMA 2020 & Nigerian Contract Law
commercial_law.rule: An indemnity clause that is unlimited in scope — covering all losses, liabilities, costs, and third-party claims without any financial cap — creates potentially ruinous exposure for a Nigerian SMB, particularly where the indemnity is one-directional and does not extend to the other party's own negligence or breach.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Cap all indemnity obligations at the total contract value or the sum of fees paid in the preceding 12 months. Exclude consequential losses, loss of profit, and indirect damages. Ensure the indemnity is mutual — if you indemnify the supplier, the supplier must equally indemnify you.
red_flags: indemnify on a full indemnity basis

commercial_law.topic: Excessive Interest Rate on Overdue Payments
commercial_law.statute: Nigerian Contract Law & Money Lenders Act
commercial_law.rule: Interest rates on overdue commercial invoices exceeding 5% per month (60% per annum) approach money-lending territory and are challengeable as penalties under Nigerian law. Self-serving labels such as 'not a penalty' or 'genuine pre-estimate' do not automatically shield compound interest clauses from judicial scrutiny. Nigerian courts apply the Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre test.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Replace compounding monthly interest with a simple annual rate not exceeding the CBN Monetary Policy Rate plus 10%. Cap total interest payable at 20-25% of the original invoice value to limit exposure.

commercial_law.statute: FCCPA 2018 & Nigerian Contract Law
commercial_law.rule: A contract that automatically renews at a higher price tier or with expanded obligations, without requiring the weaker party's affirmative consent, is an unfair commercial term. Evergreen clauses that reset minimum-purchase obligations on each renewal without an opt-out window are particularly burdensome.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Insert a minimum 60-day notice window before any auto-renewal date, during which either party can give written notice of non-renewal. Price escalation on renewal must be agreed in writing, not automatic.
red_flags: renewed at the then-current price list

commercial_law.statute: Nigerian Contract Law (Consideration & Mutuality)
commercial_law.rule: A clause permitting one party to amend, vary, or add to the contract terms at any time, with continued performance by the other party constituting acceptance, lacks the consideration and mutual assent required under Nigerian contract law for valid variation. Such clauses are commonly used to gradually worsen the weaker party's position post-signing.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Replace with: 'This Agreement may only be amended by a written instrument signed by duly authorized representatives of both parties.' Any 'continued performance equals acceptance' mechanism must be deleted.
red_flags: sole right to amend this agreement
may vary these terms at any time

commercial_law.topic: Broad Force Majeure Favouring Stronger Party
commercial_law.statute: Nigerian Contract Law & Common Law
commercial_law.rule: A force majeure clause that is drafted broadly to excuse only the supplier/stronger party, or that includes non-genuine events (market fluctuations, currency changes, government policy) as force majeure, allows the stronger party to escape obligations opportunistically. Both parties should benefit equally, and only genuinely unforeseeable events should qualify.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Ensure force majeure applies equally to both parties. Exclude currency devaluation, price changes, and foreseeable supply issues from the definition. Insert a 30-day maximum duration after which the other party may terminate without penalty.
red_flags: force majeure event excuses the supplier
including but not limited to changes in law
supplier shall not be liable for

commercial_law.topic: Waiver of Right to Dispute / Audit
commercial_law.statute: Nigerian Contract Law & Evidence Act 2011
commercial_law.rule: A clause preventing the weaker party from auditing accounts, disputing invoices after a short window (e.g., 7 days), or challenging supplier calculations effectively removes access to evidence and remedies. Nigerian courts treat such clauses as unconscionable where they prevent the weaker party from establishing basic facts about the debt.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Insist on a minimum 30-day invoice dispute window, a right to audit supplier records relevant to the contract at reasonable notice, and a clause that a disputed invoice does not become payable until the dispute is resolved.
red_flags: right to dispute an invoice is waived
disputes must be raised within 7 days
deemed correct unless objected to within

commercial_law.statute: Nigerian Contract Law & Hadley v Baxendale Principles
commercial_law.rule: While consequential loss exclusions are common in commercial contracts, a clause that excludes consequential losses for the supplier only — while leaving the distributor/buyer fully exposed to consequential claims — is an unfair and unenforceable asymmetric term. The exclusion must be mutual to be equitable.
commercial_law.negotiation_tip: Accept a mutual consequential loss exclusion. Reject any one-sided version. If you are the buyer/distributor, ensure lost profits arising from supply failure are either recoverable or hedged via a capped direct damages floor.
red_flags: no liability for loss of profit
consequential loss is excluded for the supplier only
supplier shall not be liable for any loss of revenue

employment_law.rule: Under the Nigerian Labour Act, a worker is entitled to minimum notice before termination (1 day for daily workers, 1 week for monthly workers, etc). Summary dismissal is only justified for gross misconduct. Contracts cannot lawfully exclude this right.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Ensure your employment contract specifies at least 1-month notice for senior roles, and clearly defines what constitutes 'gross misconduct' to avoid arbitrary termination.

employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004, Section 7
employment_law.rule: Deductions from wages are only lawful if authorized by statute, court order, or written agreement with the employee specifying the purpose. Unauthorized deductions constitute a criminal offence under the Labour Act.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Do not sign any clause allowing blanket deductions. Any deduction clause must specify the exact amount, purpose, and your right to dispute.

employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004 & Nigerian Contract Law
employment_law.rule: Training repayment clauses are only enforceable if: (a) the training expenditure was genuine and documented, (b) the repayment amount is proportionate and reduces pro-rata over time, and (c) the employee was given a meaningful opportunity to negotiate before signing. A flat repayment demand regardless of tenure length is a penalty clause.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Negotiate a declining repayment schedule (e.g., 100% if you leave within 6 months, 50% within 12 months, 0% after 18 months). Insist on seeing the actual training cost receipts before signing any bond.
red_flags: repay all costs if you resign
cost of training shall be recovered

employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004 & Restraint of Trade Doctrine
employment_law.rule: Garden leave clauses (requiring the employee to stay away from work during notice while remaining employed) and non-solicitation clauses must be reasonable in duration and scope. Nigerian courts will not enforce them if they effectively prevent a person from working in their profession for an unreasonable period.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Limit garden leave to the actual notice period only. Non-solicitation of clients should be limited to 6 months and restricted to clients you personally dealt with — not the employer's entire client base.
red_flags: may not work during notice period

employment_law.rule: An employer cannot unilaterally vary the fundamental terms of employment (salary, role, location, hours) without the employee's consent. A clause purporting to allow the employer to vary any term at its discretion is void under the Labour Act and equivalent to a repudiatory breach.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Ensure any variation clause requires written agreement from both parties. The employer's ability to vary role or location should be subject to reasonable notice (minimum 30 days) and your right to terminate with full severance if you cannot reasonably accept the variation.
red_flags: employer may modify conditions of employment

employment_law.statute: Copyright Act 2022 & Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004
employment_law.rule: An employment clause assigning all intellectual property created by an employee — including works created in personal time, unrelated to the employer's business — to the employer goes beyond what Nigerian law permits. The Copyright Act 2022 limits employer ownership to works created in the course of employment.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Limit IP assignment to works created 'in the course of employment and using company resources.' Add an explicit carve-out: 'This clause does not apply to works created entirely in the employee's personal time and unrelated to the company's business.'
red_flags: all inventions shall belong to the employer
including works created outside working hours
personal projects shall be company property
all developments belong to the company
intellectual property created at any time

employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004 & Nigerian Employment Practice
employment_law.rule: A probationary period should typically not exceed 3–6 months. Clauses that extend probation indefinitely, reduce notice entitlements to zero during probation, or deny all statutory benefits during an excessively long probation may be void or challengeable.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Ensure probation is capped at 3 months (6 months maximum for senior roles), that at least 1-week notice applies even during probation, and that statutory benefits (pension, leave) accrue from the first day of employment.
